passage: Every Monday at Thabo's school in Johannesburg, the whole school stood for the anthem in the dusty quad. Thabo stood because Mrs Mokoena said so, the way he tied his shoes: without thinking. Mostly he thought about lunch. Then one Monday he noticed Diego, the new boy from Argentina, standing very still with his hand on his heart, even though he didn't know the words. After assembly Thabo asked, 'Why do you stand like that? It's not your anthem.' Diego shrugged. 'At home my abuelo taught me: when people sing for their country, you show respect. It's their heart.' Thabo thought of his own grandmother, who sang the anthem with tears in her eyes. The next Monday he stood still and actually listened to the words.

qa.q: Where did Diego come from?
qa.a: Argentina.

qa.q: How did Thabo feel about the anthem at first?
qa.a: Bored and indifferent; he stood without thinking and mostly thought about lunch.

qa.q: What changed the way Thabo stood?
qa.a: Diego's answer and remembering his grandmother's tears helped him see standing as respect, not just a rule.

qa.q: How does Diego see standing for another country's anthem?
qa.a: As showing respect, because the song is people's heart.

grounding: A boy who stands for the anthem only because he is told to learns from a new classmate that it is a way of showing respect.

passage: At Mohit's school, the anthem played over a crackly speaker at every morning assembly, and Mohit stood because Sir would scold anyone who didn't. His mind wandered to cricket scores. One day, Irfan's grandfather, a retired army havildar with a white moustache, came to speak at assembly. When the anthem played, the old man stood so straight and still that Mohit couldn't stop watching him. Afterwards Mohit asked, 'Why do you stand like that, even now?' The old man said, 'Because for fifty-two seconds, everyone in this country, rich or poor, stands together. It's a way of saying we respect each other.' Mohit hadn't thought of it that way. The next morning, when the speaker crackled, he stood still and thought about the whole country standing with him.

qa.q: Who came to speak at assembly?
qa.a: Irfan's grandfather, a retired army havildar.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling while watching the old man stand?
qa.a: Curious and a little moved, unable to stop watching how straight and still he stood.

qa.q: What did Mohit learn about why people stand?
qa.a: That it is a way of showing respect for each other, not just a rule to avoid being scolded.

qa.q: How does Irfan's grandfather see standing for the anthem?
qa.a: As everyone, rich or poor, standing together in respect.

grounding: A boy who stands for the anthem out of habit learns from a retired soldier that it is a shared act of respect.

passage:
Assembly note, by Rukmini Iyer, Class 5 teacher, Friday.
During the anthem this morning, Aditi and two friends in the third row started giggling at a boy whose voice cracked on a high note. Aditi's shoulders were shaking, and she kept glancing at her friends to check they were still laughing. Some of the younger children turned to look. After assembly I took Aditi aside, not to scold, but to ask. She went red. 'Everyone was laughing, Ma'am. I didn't think.' I told her that for many people in the hall the anthem matters a great deal, including some whose families served the country. She nodded slowly and said she would save her jokes for the playground. At Monday's assembly I watched; Aditi stood quietly, eyes forward.

qa.q: What made the girls giggle?
qa.a: A boy whose voice cracked on a high note.

qa.q: Why did Aditi keep glancing at her friends?
qa.a: She felt pressure to fit in and be part of the joke; she was laughing because they were.

qa.q: What did the teacher do instead of scolding?
qa.a: Took Aditi aside, asked what happened, and explained why the anthem matters to many people.

qa.q: How might the boy whose voice cracked have felt?
qa.a: Embarrassed and self-conscious hearing the giggles.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a girl giggling during the anthem because friends did, and learning why it matters to others.

passage:
Independence Day
Diary, Samir here. This morning at the flag hoisting, Madhuri whispered that the principal's hat looked like an upside-down bucket, right as the anthem started. I snorted. Then I couldn't stop. My shoulders were shaking, and I was pressing my lips together so hard they hurt. The old man next to us, Mr Bakshi from Block C, turned and looked at me. Not angry. Just sad. He was standing so straight, holding his walking stick, and I remembered Papa saying he'd been in the army for thirty years. My face burned. After the anthem I said sorry to him. He said, 'It's all right, son. Just remember it matters to some of us.' From now on I'm saving my jokes for the walk home.

qa.q: What did Madhuri say the principal's hat looked like?
qa.a: An upside-down bucket.

qa.q: How did Samir feel when Mr Bakshi looked at him?
qa.a: Ashamed and embarrassed; his face burned.

qa.q: What did Samir do after the anthem, and what does he decide?
qa.a: He apologised to Mr Bakshi and decided to save his jokes for the walk home.

qa.q: How did Mr Bakshi feel about the giggling?
qa.a: Sad rather than angry, because the anthem matters to him after thirty years in the army.

grounding: A boy writes about giggling during the anthem because a friend joked, seeing it hurt an old soldier, and saving jokes for later.

passage: On the class trip to the small town museum, the guide stopped at a faded photo of a young woman in a white sari. 'This is Sarala Bai, from right here in our town,' she said. 'When she was only sixteen, she taught poor children to read in secret at night, even when the police came looking. She said a free country needs people who can read.' Gopika stared at the photo. Sixteen. Only six years older than her. Her skin tingled all over. 'I could never be that brave,' she whispered to Irfan. 'Maybe not police-brave,' Irfan said. 'But you could teach reading.' That evening, Gopika took out her old storybooks and sat on the steps with the watchman's little daughter. They read one page together. It felt like a tiny piece of the photo.

qa.q: How old was Sarala Bai when she taught children in secret?
qa.a: Sixteen.

qa.q: How did Gopika feel looking at the photo?
qa.a: Awed and inspired; her skin tingled all over, even though she doubted she could be that brave.

qa.q: How did Gopika turn her admiration into action?
qa.a: She read a storybook with the watchman's little daughter, serving in a small way.

qa.q: How did Irfan see Gopika's worry about not being brave?
qa.a: He thought she could still help in her own way, like teaching reading.

grounding: On a museum trip a girl is awed by a local freedom fighter's story and serves in a small way by teaching a child to read.

passage:
Saturday. Chaitanya's uncle, a soldier home on leave from a post high in the mountains, told them about the snow: how he and his friends dug out a stranded bus of pilgrims in the freezing night, passing every blanket they had to the children. Chaitanya sat with his mouth open. A shiver of awe stayed with him all through dinner.
Sunday. Chaitanya kept thinking about it. 'I want to be brave like Chachu,' he told his sister Aditi. 'You're ten,' she said. 'You can't dig out buses.' 'Then what can I do?'
Wednesday. At school, Chaitanya signed up to be the morning helper for the Class 1 children at the gate, carrying bags for the smallest ones. It wasn't snow. But it felt like his own small post.

qa.q: What did Chachu and his friends dig out?
qa.a: A stranded bus of pilgrims.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya feel listening to Chachu's story?
qa.a: Full of awe; a shiver stayed with him all through dinner.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya turn awe into service?
qa.a: He became the morning helper for Class 1 children at the gate, carrying bags for the smallest ones.

qa.q: How did Aditi respond to Chaitanya wanting to be brave?
qa.a: Practically; she reminded him he was ten and couldn't dig out buses, which made him look for something he could do.

grounding: Over several days a boy awed by his soldier uncle's story finds a small way to serve at school.

passage: On Independence Day at the village school near Bikaner, the new boy, Wasim, whose family had come from a fishing town in Kerala, stood at the front and recited a poem he had written about the country: the sea he grew up beside, the desert he now lived in, the snow he had never seen. Some kids sniggered at his accent. One whispered, 'What does he know? He's not even from here.' Imran felt his cheeks burn. He had thought the same thing on Wasim's first day. But the poem had the sea and the sand and the snow all in one country. Maybe loving it didn't belong only to people from one place. After the programme, Imran walked up. 'Your poem was the best. Teach me the sea part?' Wasim grinned, relieved.

qa.q: Where did Wasim's family come from?
qa.a: A fishing town in Kerala.

qa.q: Why did Imran's cheeks burn?
qa.a: He felt ashamed, because he had once thought the same unkind thing about Wasim not being from there.

qa.q: How did Imran welcome Wasim?
qa.a: He praised the poem and asked Wasim to teach him the sea part.

qa.q: How did Wasim feel when Imran came up?
qa.a: Relieved and happy after the sniggering at his accent.

grounding: A village boy hears a classmate from another region say he loves the country, sees that love is not owned by one group, and welcomes him.

passage: In Noa's class in Sydney, everyone had to share something they loved about the country. When it was Bao's turn, he held up a photo of his family at their citizenship ceremony, all holding tiny flags. 'I love this country because it let us stay,' he said. 'I love the beaches, and the library, and that nobody laughed at my mum's English at the bank.' A kid at the back muttered, 'He only got here two years ago.' Noa had been thinking something similar. But Bao's voice had wobbled on 'let us stay', and Noa's own great-grandparents had come on a ship from Samoa. Nobody owned loving a place. At lunch, Noa sat next to Bao. 'Welcome, properly,' Noa said, and offered half a sandwich. 'Show me the library you like?'

qa.q: What did Bao's family hold in the photo?
qa.a: Tiny flags.

qa.q: What was Noa feeling when Bao's voice wobbled?
qa.a: Moved and a little ashamed of the earlier thought, remembering Noa's own great-grandparents came on a ship from Samoa.

qa.q: How did Noa welcome Bao?
qa.a: Noa sat with Bao at lunch, welcomed him properly, shared a sandwich and asked to see his favourite library.

qa.q: What was it like for Bao sharing his love for the country?
qa.a: Emotional and brave; his voice wobbled when he said the country let them stay.

grounding: A child in Australia hears a newer classmate say he loves the country, sees that belonging is not owned by one group, and welcomes him.

passage:
'You're completely wrong!' Anand Chacha thumped the table, and the dal bowls rattled.
'And you only watch one channel!' Papa shot back.
Sangeeta shrank into her chair. They were arguing about the elections and a new road and some leader she didn't know, and both their faces were red.
After dinner, she found Chacha on the balcony. 'Chacha, do you and Papa hate each other now?'
He laughed, surprised. 'Hate? No, beta. We just think differently about what's good for the country.'
'But you both love the country?'
'Both of us. Very much. That's why we shout.'
'Can't you love it and not shout?'
Chacha scratched his head. 'That's a better question than anything we said at dinner.' He went inside. Sangeeta heard him say, 'Bhaiya, sorry for thumping the table.'

qa.q: What did Anand Chacha thump?
qa.a: The table.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta feel during the argument?
qa.a: Confused and frightened, shrinking into her chair as their faces went red.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta do to understand the argument?
qa.a: She calmly asked Chacha whether they hated each other and whether they both loved the country.

qa.q: How did Chacha see the argument after Sangeeta's questions?
qa.a: He saw they both love the country but think differently, and he apologised to Papa.

grounding: A girl confused by elders arguing angrily about the country asks calm questions and learns respect for the nation does not mean everyone agrees.

passage: At my cousin's wedding last winter, two of my uncles started arguing about the country so loudly that the band stopped playing. I'm Afreen. One said the government was ruining everything; the other said it was saving everything. They both looked so angry that I thought they would never speak again. I was confused. How could two people who loved the same country think such opposite things? Later, I sat with Bhupen Dada, our old neighbour, near the sweets table and asked him. He peeled an orange for me and said, 'People can love the same home and disagree about how to paint it. What matters is not tearing it down while you argue.' When I looked back, my uncles were sharing a plate of biryani. Still arguing. Just more quietly.

qa.q: What stopped when the uncles argued?
qa.a: The band stopped playing.

qa.q: How did Afreen feel watching the uncles argue?
qa.a: Confused and worried, thinking they might never speak again.

qa.q: What helped Afreen understand the disagreement?
qa.a: Sitting with Bhupen Dada and calmly asking how people who love the same country can disagree.

qa.q: How does Bhupen Dada see disagreement about the country?
qa.a: As normal, like disagreeing about how to paint the same home, as long as nobody tears it down.

grounding: A child confused by relatives arguing about the country asks an elder and learns people can love it and still disagree.

passage:
School trip note, by Ankita Sharma, Class 5 teacher, India Gate visit.
Near the war memorial, a man in a hurry dropped a chip packet and an empty bottle right beside the flower beds. Several children noticed. Tejas frowned and looked at me, then at the litter, clearly uneasy. He hesitated, then walked over, picked up both, and dropped them in the bin by the path. As the man turned back, Tejas said politely, 'Uncle, the bin's just there.' The man looked a little embarrassed and nodded. Later Tejas told me, 'It felt wrong, rubbish next to the memorial. The soldiers' names are there.' At lunch I told the class what he had done. Two other children spent the next ten minutes picking up wrappers along the path.

qa.q: What did the man drop?
qa.a: A chip packet and an empty bottle.

qa.q: Why did Tejas look uneasy?
qa.a: He felt it was wrong and disrespectful to leave rubbish next to the memorial with the soldiers' names.

qa.q: What did Tejas do?
qa.a: Picked up the litter, put it in the bin, and politely told the man the bin was just there.

qa.q: How did the man react to Tejas's reminder?
qa.a: He looked a little embarrassed and nodded.

grounding: A teacher's note records a boy who feels uneasy at litter near a memorial, picks it up and gently reminds the man.

passage:
Saturday
Diary, Ganga writing. We went to the park with the big statue of the freedom fighter holding a lamp, where a little flag flies on the pole. Zubin finished his ice lolly and tossed the stick and wrapper right at the statue's feet. Nobody said anything. I felt uneasy, like a pebble in my shoe. I didn't want to sound bossy. But the flowers around the statue were already full of rubbish. I picked up Zubin's wrapper and said, 'Let's use the bin, na? It's his park too.' I pointed at the statue. Zubin laughed, a bit embarrassed, and then picked up two more wrappers himself. We found five in all. Tomorrow I'm bringing a bag.

qa.q: What did Zubin toss at the statue's feet?
qa.a: The ice lolly stick and wrapper.

qa.q: How did Ganga feel when nobody said anything?
qa.a: Uneasy, like a pebble in a shoe, but worried about sounding bossy.

qa.q: How did Ganga remind Zubin without being bossy?
qa.a: By picking up the wrapper and lightly suggesting the bin, joking that it was the statue's park too.

qa.q: How did Zubin respond?
qa.a: A bit embarrassed at first, then helpful; he picked up two more wrappers himself.

grounding: A child uneasy at litter by a freedom fighter's statue picks it up and gently reminds a friend.

passage: When I turned ten, my mother, Nirmala, started giving me pocket money every Sunday: two crisp twenty-rupee notes. I'm Abhinav, and I felt so grown up, keeping them in my own zip pouch. The first few weeks I spent them on the first thing I saw, gummies and stickers. Then one night I woke at four and saw Amma coming home from her night shift at the hospital, still in her nurse's uniform, rubbing her feet at the kitchen table. I thought about my forty rupees. That Sunday, when she handed them over, I said, 'Thank you, Amma,' and actually meant it. I bought a pencil I needed and kept the rest for her birthday. When I gave her a jasmine gajra, she laughed and cried at the same time.

qa.q: How much pocket money did Abhinav get each Sunday?
qa.a: Two crisp twenty-rupee notes.

qa.q: What did Abhinav feel after seeing Amma come home from her night shift?
qa.a: Grateful and moved, seeing how hard she worked.

qa.q: How did Abhinav's choices change after that night?
qa.a: Abhinav thanked Amma sincerely, bought something needed, and kept the rest for her birthday gift.

qa.q: How did Amma feel receiving the jasmine gajra?
qa.a: Touched and happy; she laughed and cried at the same time 🤍

grounding: A child who feels grown up getting pocket money comes to appreciate the parent's hard work behind it and spends thoughtfully.

passage:
From Mehak's family notebook, Sunday.
Today Divyansh got his first weekly pocket money, a fifty-rupee note, and walked around the flat holding it like a certificate. 'I'm grown up now,' he announced. By evening he had counted it eleven times. On the way to the market with his father, he stopped at the toy stall, then at the samosa cart, then put the note back in his pocket. At dinner he asked, 'Papa, how many hours do you work for fifty rupees?' His father told him honestly. Divyansh went quiet. Later he told me he had decided to buy a birthday card for his grandmother and keep the rest in his tin until he knew what he really wanted. He said, 'Thank you for the money, Mummy,' twice.

qa.q: How many times did Divyansh count the note?
qa.a: Eleven times.

qa.q: How did Divyansh feel holding his first pocket money?
qa.a: Proud and grown up, holding it like a certificate.

qa.q: What did Divyansh's question to Papa lead to?
qa.a: He understood the work behind the money, thanked his parents, and chose carefully what to spend it on.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt answering Divyansh's question?
qa.a: Pleased that Divyansh was curious about the effort behind the money.

grounding: A mother's notebook records her son's first pocket money, his pride, and his growing gratitude for the work behind it.

passage: 'Chinmay, you spent your whole birthday money on that flashing top and now it's broken? Let your Manoj Mama tell you about the village fair. I was eight, and my Ajoba gave me five whole rupees, a fortune then. The very first stall had a tin monkey that clapped cymbals. I bought it in one breath. Five rupees, gone. By the time we reached the giant wheel, the monkey's key had snapped. I had nothing left for the ride, or the jalebi, or anything. I cried behind a tent. Ajoba didn't scold. He just said, "Next fair, walk round the whole fair once before you buy." The next year I did. I bought a little bamboo flute I played for ten years. Waiting one round taught me what I really wanted.'

qa.q: What did young Manoj buy at the first stall?
qa.a: A tin monkey that clapped cymbals.

qa.q: How did young Manoj feel behind the tent?
qa.a: Regretful and sad, with nothing left for the ride or the jalebi after the monkey broke.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped Manoj the next year?
qa.a: Walking round the whole fair once before buying, which led him to a flute he played for ten years.

qa.q: How did Ajoba respond to Manoj's tears?
qa.a: Gently, without scolding, offering a simple idea for next time.

grounding: An uncle recalls spending all his fair money in a moment, regretting it, and learning to wait before buying.

passage: The school trip bus would leave the mall in fifteen minutes, and Tarun had his whole month's pocket money in his pocket. In the first shop, a glowing slime kit caught his eye. He grabbed it and paid, every last rupee, in under a minute. His heart raced with delight. Then, walking back past the bookshop, he saw the comic his little sister Kiran had wanted for months, with a sticker saying 'Last copy'. He had promised to bring her something. Tarun's stomach sank. The slime suddenly looked sticky and silly. On the bus, he stared out of the window. 'Next time,' he muttered, 'I'll look at everything once before I buy anything.' At home, he gave Kiran half the slime. She squealed anyway.

qa.q: What caught Tarun's eye in the first shop?
qa.a: A glowing slime kit.

qa.q: How did Tarun feel when he saw the comic?
qa.a: Regretful and disappointed; his stomach sank because he had nothing left for Kiran.

qa.q: What did Tarun decide for next time?
qa.a: To look at everything once before buying anything.

qa.q: How did Kiran react to half the slime?
qa.a: Delighted; she squealed anyway.

grounding: On a short school trip a boy spends all his pocket money in a minute, then regrets it and decides to look before buying next time.

passage: For seven months, Anders dropped every coin from his birthday, his tooth money and his dog-walking into a jam jar on his shelf in Leeds. He wanted one thing: the willow cricket bat in the sports shop window, the one with the red grip. Some weeks the jar barely changed. Once he nearly spent it all on a video game, then put the money back. On a Saturday in April, he counted it on the carpet with Mei from next door. Enough. They walked to the shop together, and Anders paid with his own crinkled notes and a heap of coins. The shopkeeper counted patiently. Walking home with the bat on his shoulder, Anders felt taller than the lamp posts. 'You waited forever,' Mei said. 'Worth it,' he grinned.

qa.q: Where did Anders keep his savings?
qa.a: In a jam jar on his shelf.

qa.q: How did Anders feel walking home with the bat?
qa.a: Deeply proud, as if taller than the lamp posts.

qa.q: What helped Anders reach the bat?
qa.a: Patience over seven months, including putting the money back when a video game tempted him.

qa.q: How did Mei see Anders's long wait?
qa.a: As a very long wait; she was struck that he had waited forever.

grounding: A boy in England saves for months and buys a cricket bat with his own money, feeling deep pride in his patience.

passage: At the cricket academy nets, Vikas unzipped a brand-new bat cover, and the other boys crowded round. 'Did your dad buy it?' someone asked. 'No,' Vikas said, and his chest swelled. 'I did.' For five months he had saved his pocket money and his birthday and Diwali money, skipping the samosas after practice. Saurabh Sir came over and weighed the bat in his hands. 'Good balance. You chose well.' Then he said, 'Five months? That's patience. The same patience you need for a long innings.' Vikas grinned so wide his cheeks hurt. That day he batted slower and more carefully than ever and stayed in for twenty-three balls, his longest.

qa.q: How long had Vikas saved?
qa.a: Five months.

qa.q: How did Vikas feel saying 'I did'?
qa.a: Proud; his chest swelled.

qa.q: What did Saurabh Sir connect saving to?
qa.a: The same patience needed for a long innings.

qa.q: How might the other boys see Vikas's bat?
qa.a: With admiration and curiosity, crowding round and asking who bought it.

grounding: At a cricket academy a boy proudly shows a bat he saved for, and his coach links that patience to batting.

passage: At the weekly haat in their village near Hisar, Kiran bought a toy car, a bag of jalebis and a shiny water bottle, all in ten minutes. His father worked in Dubai and sent money home every month. Vikas had four rupees in his pocket and a pang in his chest. He had never had a toy car that wasn't borrowed. Walking home past the mustard fields, he kicked a stone hard. Then Kiran said, 'Can you ask your Dadaji to help me make a kite like yours? Mine from the shop breaks every time.' Vikas thought of Dadaji's hands splitting bamboo and gluing paper, and of their kite that flew higher than anyone's. Families were different. His had something too. 'Come on Sunday,' he said. 'Bring the jalebis.'

qa.q: What did Kiran buy at the haat?
qa.a: A toy car, a bag of jalebis and a shiny water bottle.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling as he kicked the stone?
qa.a: Envious and a bit sad, with a pang that he had never had a toy car of his own.

qa.q: What helped Vikas let go of the comparison?
qa.a: Remembering that families differ and valuing what he has, like Dadaji's kite-making.

qa.q: How does Kiran see Vikas's family?
qa.a: As having something special, since Kiran wants Dadaji's help to make a strong kite.

grounding: A village boy feels a pang of envy at a friend's pocket money, then remembers families differ and values what he has.

passage: At school in Manchester, Jin always had money for the tuck shop: crisps, fizzy sweets, a new pack of trading cards every week. Kofi got three pounds a week and usually saved it. Watching Jin rip open yet another pack, Kofi felt a sharp pang. At home he grumbled, 'Jin gets loads more pocket money. It's not fair.' His mum was stitching a hem. 'Every family's different, Kofi. Jin's parents both work long hours, and he's with his childminder till seven.' Kofi hadn't known that. On Saturday morning he and his dad fixed the chain on his bike in the yard, laughing, oil on their hands. Afterwards he thought about Jin at the childminder's. Maybe he would invite Jin to fix bikes next Saturday.

qa.q: How much pocket money did Kofi get?
qa.a: Three pounds a week.

qa.q: What was Kofi feeling as Jin ripped open another pack?
qa.a: Envious, with a sharp pang, feeling it was unfair.

qa.q: What helped Kofi value what he had?
qa.a: Mum reminding him that families differ, and his Saturday morning fixing the bike with Dad.

qa.q: What might Jin's weekdays be like, from what Mum said?
qa.a: Long, with his parents working late and Jin at the childminder's till seven.

grounding: A boy envious of a friend's bigger pocket money learns families differ and comes to value his own time with his father.
